planting.note: Divide suckers in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost danger has passed; Steroidal Giant is a robust selection with markedly larger leaves and taller stature than the straight species, so allow extra space — 8-10 feet on all sides. Cut to ground after frost in zone 8; it rebounds vigorously from the root.

directions: Divide underground stolons or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Steroidal Giant is a selection of rice paper plant introduced through the nursery trade and prized for producing even larger, bolder, more deeply lobed palmate leaves than the species — often exceeding 3 feet across — on correspondingly taller and more vigorous stems that can reach 10-15 feet or more in a single season in favorable conditions. Like the species, the felted undersides of the leaves are a contrasting silver-gray, and it spreads steadily by underground stolons to form expanding colonies, which can be managed by mowing around the perimeter. In zone 8, top growth is killed by frost but the plant rebounds vigorously from underground stolons each spring, quickly regaining dramatic jungle-like stature by mid-summer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Spring Purple benefits from a sheltered position to protect early blooms from late frosts and to show off the purple-flushed new growth without wind scorch.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Spring Purple is a selection of Chinese winter hazel valued for its emerging foliage, which unfurls flushed with a deep purple-bronze cast before gradually greening as the leaves mature through late spring. Like the species, it produces long, pendulous racemes of soft yellow, lightly fragrant flowers in late winter or very early spring before the leaves emerge, each drooping chain resembling a string of small yellow bells. The large, boldly veined, heart-shaped leaves that follow color yellow in fall. One of the more cold-tolerant Corylopsis selections, surviving reliably to zone 6 and worth trying in sheltered zone 5 microclimates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Wisley Red benefits from a sheltered position to protect early blooms from late frosts and to best display the red-tinged new leaves and calyces.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wisley Red, selected at the RHS garden at Wisley, is a Chinese winter hazel cultivar notable for red-tinged new leaves and flower calyces that add an extra layer of color to the late-winter display beyond the species' soft yellow, lightly fragrant flowers. Each drooping raceme of 15-20 small bell-shaped flowers opens before the leaves emerge, and the large, boldly veined, heart-shaped foliage that follows turns yellow in fall. One of the more cold-tolerant Corylopsis selections, surviving reliably to zone 6 and worth trying in sheltered zone 5 microclimates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Krauter Vesuvius blooms very early in spring — often in February — with single pale pink flowers just before the deep purple-black foliage emerges. Among the darkest-leaved purple plum selections, and largely fruitless, reducing litter and volunteer seedlings compared to the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Krauter Vesuvius is one of the darkest-foliaged purple-leaf plum cultivars, unfurling deep purple-black leaves that hold their near-black color through the entire growing season with far less summer fading toward bronze-green than many other purple plum selections. Single, pale pink flowers open very early in spring — often in February in zones 7-9 — before the leaves emerge, followed by an oval, rounded crown of dramatic dark foliage that makes it one of the most striking specimen and accent trees in residential landscaping. It sets little to no fruit compared with the species and green-leaved cultivars, reducing cleanup and self-sown seedlings. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15-25 years) but very fast-growing and reliably floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Thundercloud blooms very early in spring — often in February — with single light pink flowers just before the reddish-purple foliage emerges. The most widely planted of the purple-leaf plum cultivars in American landscaping.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Thundercloud is the most widely planted purple-leaf plum cultivar in North America, valued for single, light pink spring flowers that open very early — often in February in zones 7-9 — just before the reddish-purple foliage emerges, which then deepens to a rich dark purple through summer before fading somewhat by fall. Its rounded, dense crown and reliable floriferousness make it a mainstay flowering and accent tree for residential landscapes, street plantings, and mixed borders. Small, round, dark red plums are produced in summer and are edible, though they are typically sparse and secondary to the ornamental display. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15-25 years) but very fast-growing; can self-sow in mild climates.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess White follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and blooming in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess White is a pure white-flowered selection of the showy winter-growing Cape sorrel, producing from winter through spring an extended succession of large (1.5-2 inch), flat-faced, funnel-shaped flowers with a contrasting yellow center, rising above compact, clover-like, dark-green foliage in a continuous, profuse bloom display that can last 3-4 months of winter and early spring. The flowers are substantially larger than most Cape oxalis species, giving the plant a presence disproportionate to its small bulb size. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it provides a bright, low-maintenance, winter-through-spring color display that requires almost no attention — plant the bulbs in fall, enjoy the flowers from winter through April, water withheld in summer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Wilson's Wonder is a compact Leucadendron salignum selection popular in the cut-foliage trade for its colorful branch-tip bracts. Never use standard fertilizer, which is toxic to proteas at normal phosphorus levels.

directions: Wilson's Wonder is a more compact Leucadendron salignum cultivar grown alongside 'Safari Sunset' and 'Cloudbank Ginny' in the international cut-foliage trade, valued for its dense, tidy habit and colorful red-flushed bracts that develop at the branch tips as temperatures cool, brightening through fall and winter. The plant itself is a bushy, upright shrub with narrow, leathery gray-green leaves that recede visually behind the colorful bract clusters. Like other Leucadendron salignum selections, it demands sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; standard garden fertilizers containing normal phosphate levels can quickly kill it, so use a protea-formulated low-phosphorus feed or none at all. Cut stems for arrangements throughout the cool season, and shape the plant lightly after the main color display fades to keep growth dense and floriferous.
